Plus: The vote against data centers | Thursday, November 05, 2026
 
View in browser
 
Presented By Kalshi
 
Axios Markets
By Emily Peck and Matt Phillips · Nov 05, 2026

👋 Good morning! Markets are still adjusting to the blue tsunami that swept polls across the nation, rocking the AI trade — possibly, if somewhat counterintuitively, for the better. More on that below.

📈📉 S&P 500 futures are up this morning after the index posted its best day since early August yesterday; Nasdaq futures are in the red.

  • The yield on the 10-year Treasury note is down to 4.88% after a rally in bonds driven by relief (remember yields move in the opposite direction of price) and the recent decline in oil prices. Recall: A month ago, yields were at 5.3%.

Today, a look at how the political backlash to data centers could shake up the AI trade.

Here we go! In 1,120 words, a 4-minute read.

 
 
1 big thing: The AI pause that refreshes
 
Data:FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

Voters clearly put the brakes on the AI build-out this week, but the biggest tech companies kept on rolling.

Why it matters: The rally in the shares of the likes of Microsoft and Amazon reflects a growing realization on Wall Street that a slowdown in the AI race may not be such a bad thing.

  • If companies can put off enormous spending commitments, they get to show healthier cash flows, avoid financing costs and possibly sidestep risky investments.

State of play: The Big Tech hyperscalers were among the biggest winners in yesterday's post-election relief rally: Microsoft was up 6.7%, Amazon, 6.1%, and Alphabet, 3.3%.

  • These are companies with businesses that generate a lot of cash doing things like selling advertising or cloud computing or software and don't absolutely need to rapidly become AI companies.
  • "Delays may frustrate, but they also make it less likely that trillions of dollars are invested in equipment at risk of becoming obsolete or depreciating faster than its financiers expected," the Financial Times Lex column noted.

Yes, but: Not all hyperscalers. Oracle closed down nearly 2% yesterday. And, over the long term, the challenges facing smaller AI firms could blow back on the big ones.

  • Those challenges might entail a slowdown in profits for companies that have had soaring sales from supplying the "picks and shovels" of the AI trade — things like fiber-optic connectors, servers and memory storage devices.
  • The market seemed to be pricing that outlook in yesterday.
Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios Visuals

The neoclouds — smaller data center operators — also stumbled.

  • These companies have borrowed a lot of money to build data centers and buy semiconductors. Slowdowns in construction mean delays in earning revenue while they're paying interest on that debt.
Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

What to watch: While most 2027 data center construction isn't likely to be affected, 37.5 gigawatts of planned 2028 capacity could face pauses and another 15 gigawatts could face "conditions," JPMorgan's Michael Cembalest noted yesterday.

  • "While pauses are the more impactful outcome," he wrote, "conditions can be onerous: requiring data centers to pay grid costs to protect ratepayers, ending tax incentives, imposing water limits, setting requirements for onsite backup power, mandating labor requirements and banning non-disclosure agreements during permitting."
 
 
2. The anti-bubble case for a slowdown
 
Data: U.S. Census Bureau, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

Slowing down the AI capex mania could be overall positive for the economy, a range of economists and investors have argued.

  • It could ease "overheating risk in the next year or two and plausibly extend the AI investment cycle," Evercore's Krishna Guha wrote. "This will help keep the whole economy demand and supply in balance without many more rate hikes."
  • The slowdown could take some of the air out of what had been looking awfully bubbly. "Anti-AI politics is bad for AI stocks in the short run but very good for preventing a bubble in the medium to long run," Substack writer Derek Thompson posted.

Zoom in: It could also be a relief for the bond market, because it would mean less new debt competing for investors' money — potentially easing upward pressure on borrowing costs, Andrew Szczurowski, strategic income portfolio manager at Morgan Stanley Investment Management, told Axios before the election.

  • He also said that at some point soon investors may stop rewarding tech companies for spending heavily on AI:
  • "You get to a point where investors on the equity and bond side are no longer ... giving you applause for how much you're spending."

Reality check: The boom in data center construction has been enormous and is driving economic growth, and so far the slow down is mostly theoretical.

  • The annualized value of data center construction reached roughly $96 billion in September 2026, up from around $60 billion earlier this year and less than $20 billion in early 2023.

The bottom line: While there will be some negative impacts, in the long run — to borrow a line from an old Coca-Cola ad — this could be the AI pause that refreshes.

3. Voters deliver "AI earthquake"
By Maria Curi
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Stock: Getty Images

 

Voters showed deep distrust of the AI race Tuesday, approving dozens of data center moratoriums and electing a raft of candidates who favor slowing a $10 trillion build-out, including in Texas — the epicenter of the boom.

Why it matters: In an election that hinged on an affordability crisis for many Americans, voters made it clear they view Silicon Valley's AI ambitions not as a technological miracle, but as a resource-draining threat to their wallets and communities.

  • The results were a warning shot to some of the nation's wealthiest and most powerful executives, many of whom are already working on ways to build a more palatable version of the revolution they are dead set on winning.

"What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake," Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, told Axios. "Voters just sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers."

Driving the news: Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa's surprise victory in the Texas governor's race fundamentally scrambles the math for the AI buildout.

  • Hinojosa campaigned on keeping a moratorium on data center construction in place until the state passes legislation tackling impacts on water, electricity, air and property rights in the legislative session that ends in mid-2027.
  • While most U.S. data centers expected in 2027 are already under construction, a hold for more than six months would bring extended delays in Texas, which accounts for 41% of new U.S. capacity in 2028, according to the research firm SemiAnalysis.
  • Democrats won all three of the states that follow Texas for new data center capacity, including Ohio, Georgia and Arizona. The winners in Ohio and Georgia favor restrictive policies, although it's not yet clear how those will take shape.

Between the lines: All told, nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity could face delays, although most political analysts don't see Democrats permanently blocking construction.
